Chapter 7: Healing Old Wounds—The Power of Presence.
You know, old wounds have this uncanny way of showing up—right at the dinner table. Maybe it’s a memory from childhood, a moment of rejection, or just that lingering sting from something that happened years ago. All of these can quietly sneak into the way we eat, even if we don’t realize it.
The truth is, our history really does shape our relationship with food. Think about it—the pain we haven’t healed often turns into a hunger we just can’t seem to satisfy.
Picture this: as a kid, you’re told to clean your plate, even when you’re already full. So, you learn to ignore what your body’s telling you. You end up eating for approval, not for hunger. Fast forward to adulthood, and maybe you find yourself finishing meals out of pure habit—unable to leave anything behind. That old lesson? It’s still there, guiding your choices without you even noticing.
What if you could approach those old wounds with presence? That’s what this chapter is all about—bringing real awareness to the moments when your past is influencing your present. It’s about noticing those patterns and offering a bit of compassion to the parts of yourself that are still hurting.
Most of us try to outrun our pain, right? We use food as a distraction, hoping the hurt will just disappear. But pain doesn’t vanish—it simply waits for another chance to be heard.
Let me share a story. There was a woman who noticed she always wanted to binge after a tough conversation with her mom. Those feelings of not being good enough, the longing for approval—it was so overwhelming that eating felt like the only way to cope. But once she saw this pattern, she started to pause. Before reaching for food, she’d ask herself, “What am I really feeling?” Little by little, she found new ways to comfort herself—maybe by journaling, calling a friend, or just sitting quietly with her emotions.
She discovered something powerful: healing old wounds takes presence. It means being willing to feel the pain, instead of numbing it. It means offering kindness to the hurting parts of yourself. You might be surprised by how much things change when you start meeting pain with compassion. The urge to eat for comfort? It fades. And in its place, there’s a quiet sense of peace.
Remember, healing isn’t about erasing the past. It’s about seeing how the past shapes you today—and choosing to respond with care. Most people are amazed at how different life feels when they stop running from their pain. Eating becomes less about escape, and more about real nourishment.
Now, this journey toward healing isn’t easy. It takes courage, patience, and a willingness to feel a little uncomfortable at times. But here’s the beautiful part—it offers freedom. Freedom to choose, to care for yourself, and to create new patterns. So many people don’t realize they actually have this power.
By bringing presence to your old wounds, you can start to heal—not just your relationship with food, but your relationship with yourself.
